content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to battle memorization overfitting problem in meta learning using causality. The authors view the process of meta-learning through the lens of causality which produces several causal graphs i.e. Fig. 1(b) for the general one and Fig. 2 (a-d) for special cases. Based on the causal graphs, the authors use 'front-door' adjustment and propose two algorithms MAML Dropout and MAML Bins.
content.main_review:
The memorization overfitting problem is worthy investigating, and using causality for meta-learning makes sense. The experiment is good. 

The meta-learning procedure is a dynamic process, and thus it might be better to use a temporal model instead of a static model. 

The authors stated that 'directly cutting the causal relationship between $Y$ and $\theta'$ via backdoor adjustment is impossible', and then 'Despite this, we still propose two kinds of deconfounded methods applying to MAML'. That sounds self-contradictory. 

---Post-rebuttal---
I am happy with the responses from the authors and have increased the score.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think this direction is worthy exploring. The paper's idea is interesting and the experiment results are promising. The two algorithms can be better motivated and explained, which can perhaps be addressed in the camera-ready version. I am leaning towards accepting the paper.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper2418 by Reviewer STG8

content.title: Response to Reviewer STG8
content.comment:
Thanks a lot for your constructive comments. Here we provide our response to your concerns as below. Please kindly let us know if you have further concerns.

#### Q1: a temporal model instead of a static model for the meta-learning procedure

> Our causal graph is illustrated on the basis of only two outer-loop steps (i.e., $\theta'\rightarrow \theta$), though the whole meta-training process is indeed dynamic by constantly repeating the two steps. Our proposed deconfounding methods, accordingly, are applied in each step throughout the whole meta-training process.

#### Q2: self-contradictory between 'directly cutting the causal relationship between $Y$ and $\theta'$ via backdoor adjustment is impossible', and 'Despite this, we still propose two kinds of deconfounded methods applying to MAML'

> We apologize for any misunderstanding here. 
>
> -  By "directly cutting the causal relationship between $Y$ and $\theta'$ via backdoor adjustment is impossible", we mean that the **backdoor adjustment** is not applicable to meta-learning, provided that the two edges $Y\rightarrow\theta$ and $Y\rightarrow\theta'$ always change simultaneously. 
> - By "Despite this, we still propose two kinds of deconfounded methods applying to MAML", we mean that we resort to the other way of deconfounding meta-learning, i.e., via **frontdoor adjustment**.

replying_to: Replying to Minimizing Memorization in Meta-learning: A Causal Perspective
display_title: Official Review of Paper2418 by Reviewer 7TwH

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper addresses the undesirable memorization problem in the context of gradient-based meta-learning, where the meta-learning knowledge obtained as a result of memorizing all meta-training tasks yields poor generalization and is detrimental to task specific adaptation. While previous work has focused on regularization-based and augmentation-based solutions to prevent the memorization of all meta-training tasks, the authors argue these methods and their benefits are still not well understood and propose a causal perspective of meta-learning in a unified causal framework. In this context the authors identify the universal label space of the base model as the confounding factor of memorization causing spurious correlations between initializations learnt in different meta-training steps. Informed by this analysis, the authors demonstrate why existing meta-learning overfitting solutions work, and propose two deconfounder approaches to address the issue of memorization, namely i) sampling multiple versions of the meta-knowledge via dropout (MAML-Dropout), and ii) grouping the meta-knowledge into bins (MAML-Bins).
content.main_review:
Strengths:

The paper addresses an important issue (poor generalization due to undesirable memorization overfitting in meta-learning) and aims to clarify why existing solutions work, which is an important gap lacking solid theoretical understanding in the literature.

The novelty of the paper lies in the causal perspective the authors adopt for understanding gradient-based meta-learning, bridging together the separate research areas of causal inference and meta-learning. 

The proposed causal graph framework allows authors to identify the universal label space as the confounder behind undesirable memorization. In the context of their proposed causal framework, it is possible to explain from the perspective of deconfounder approaches why existing regularizer-based and augmentation-based solutions work. 

The argument that the universal label space Y leads to spurious correlations is well-argumented and convincingly explained in the context of the causal framework. The change in semantic meaning of task labels that vary from task to task is indeed problematic and additionally affects labels Y. 

The authors break the path from \theta’ (confounded past meta-knowledge) and the task adapted model \phi through frontdoor adjustment deconfounding in the causal graph and propose two simple methods to implement this approach (MAML-Dropout and MAML-Bins)

Their proposed deconfounding methods are compatible with and work on top of existing meta-learning algorithms, displaying improved performance

The paper is well-motivated, well-framed in the context of the literature, informative and well-written; figures serve to illustrate the content and arguments of the paper.


Weaknesses:

Not clear from the paper itself to what extent the current work is different from past works of Bengio et al (2020) and Yue et al (2020) that also combine meta-learning with causality, the authors should aim to better clarify the differences. In addition, the authors do not clearly describe the difference between MAML-Dropout and DropGrad (Tseng et al, 2020) - is it just adding dropout layers in the forward network in the meta-training phase? 

The paper lacks important details about the choice of hyper-parameters, in particular:
a) How do you determine the dropout rate for MAML-Dropout in your experiments?
b) How do you determine the ideal number of bins to split the value range of training data into for MAML-Bins?

What is the additional computational overload caused by the introduction of clustering in the MAML-Bins inner step? 

In their experiments the authors select which method to report results for (whether MAML-Dropout, MAML-Bins, or their combination) rather arbitrarily without clear motivation and comparison among these methods. For example, in Sections 5.1, 5.3 and 5.4 the authors claim that  both methods have positive effects and that using them together (MAML-Dropout + MAML-Bins) achieves the best performance. However they contradict this statement in Section 5.2 where they only report results for MAML-Dropout claiming MAML-Bins brings additional noise.

Figure 3: how do authors explain that MAML-Dropout is in general outperforming MAML-Bins? There is no discussion included in the paper about this.

Long-range question: What insights can be drawn from this study that could be useful in combating learner overfitting, and how to leverage those?

Typos: 
Section 2.1: “​​In outer-loop optimizaiton,”
Section 3.2: “We details the auxiliary task in Appendix C.”
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper is generally sound and convincing, and addresses an important problem in the literature. Combining meta-learning with causal inference to combat memorization overfitting seems a promising approach that can alleviate shortcomings of existing meta-learning methods and opens new research directions. The claims are generally well-motivated both theoretically and empirically.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 7TwH (2/2)
content.comment:
#### Q4: additional computation overhead caused by the clustering in the MAML-Bins inner-step

> - Assigning a bin label to each example by clustering for classification tasks and by interval splitting for regression tasks is a **pre-processing step**, as we have detailed in Appendix C and the next-to-last paragraph in Section 3.2. 
> - With bin labels obtained in the above pre-processing step, we simply incorporate an auxiliary bin classification loss in the MAML-Bins inner-step (see Eq.(5)), which does not incur additional computation overhead.

#### Q5: applying MAML-Dropout+MAML-Bins in Section 5.1/5.3/5.4 vs. applying MAML-Dropout in Section 5.2

> - The prerequisite for the success of MAML-Bins is a globally shared set of bins, which are invariant to different tasks. 
> - Generally under a standard non-mutually exclusive setting (Section 5.1/5.3/5.4) which meets the prerequisite easily, both methods (MAML-Dropout and MAML-Bins) will be applied. Figure 3 advocates the benefits of leveraging both methods in alleviating the memorization.
> - The drug dataset in Section 5.2, however, is an exception setting that **fails to meet the prerequisite**. As drug activity prediction is a regression problem, a quick recipe for obtaining a set of bins is to split the $y$ values into several intervals, following the next-to-last paragraph in Section 3.2. Unfortunately, the meanings of such a set of bins vary from task to task: due to differences in measurement facilities and conditions [1], the bin (7,8) containing those compounds with the highest bio-activity in one task likely corresponds to only the second or the third-highest bio-active compounds in the other task. This is also the reason why the literature on drug activity prediction takes Pearson coefficient (R2) as the evaluation metric instead of MSE. Consequently, it is invalid to apply MAML-Bins. 
>
> [1] (Martin et al. 2019) Eric J Martin, Valery R Polyakov, Xiang-Wei Zhu, Li Tian, Prasenjit Mukherjee, and Xin Liu. All assay-max2 pqsar: activity predictions as accurate as four-concentration ic50s for 8558 novartis assays. Journal of chemical information and modeling, 59(10):4450–4459, 2019.

#### Q6: MAML-Dropout > MAML-Bins?

> We thank Reviewer 7TwH's suggestion and will give more discussion on this in the revision. 
>
> - The two proposed methods sample stratification and deconfound in different manners: stratums in MAML-Dropout are $\theta$s dropping different parts of features, while stratums in MAML-Bins are different combinations of existing features represented by $\theta$. 
> - They are complementary and mutually reinforcing, as evidenced in Figure 3.
> - In general, MAML-Dropout tends to have more stratums than MAML-Bins, accounting for its better performance.

#### Q7: insights for learner overfitting

> Our work in this paper mainly focuses on the meta-training phase. However, learner overfitting happens when the meta-knowledge becomes invalid in the meta-testing phase. The domain shift between training tasks and testing tasks can be a possible reason for learner overfitting. We can also explain this kind of learner overfitting via a causal perspective.
>
> - Ideally, meta-training tasks and meta-testing tasks are sampled independently from a task distribution, which means that the real causal relationship in the meta-testing phase is $T^{train} \rightarrow \theta \rightarrow \phi_i \leftarrow T^{test}_i$. 
> - Practically, an unobserved domain shift $u$ causes a **spurious correlation** between the meta-testing task $T^{test}_i$ and the adaptive model $\phi_i$ , i.e., $T^{test}_i \leftarrow u \rightarrow T^{train} \rightarrow \theta \rightarrow \phi_i$. Here, $u$ indicates how meta-testing tasks shift from meta-training tasks.
> 
> Under this view, we believe that the causal perspective and deconfounding skills proposed in this work will lay a solid foundation for alleviating learner overfitting.

Thank you for your constructive comments. We detail our response below and have corrected the typos in our revision. Please kindly let us know if our response addresses the issues you raised.

#### Q1: differences from Bengio et al. (2020) and Yue et al. (2020)

> We will follow Reviewer 7TwH's suggestion to clarify the differences of our work from Bengio et al. (2020) and Yue et al. (2020) in more detail, besides the second paragraph of Section 4. 
>
> - The goal of Bengio et al. (2020) is to leverage a meta-learning objective to discover causal structures **for fast transfer learning**, while our objective is to leverage causation **for better meta-learning**. That is, this work and Bengio et al. (2020) solve completely different research problems. 
> - Yue et al (2020) (i.e., IFSL in Table 1 and Table 3) aims to deconfound the pre-trained knowledge **during meta-testing**, while our work aims to conquer the memorization problem which arises **during meta-training**. Consequently, Yue et al. (2020) (i.e., IFSL) cannot handle the memorization problem we focus on, as evidenced in Table 1 and Table 3.

> - DropGrad, thereby, addresses the inner-loop overfitting problem; the contribution of addressing this inner-loop overfitting towards memorization, though positive, is limited, which has been extensively validated in [1] and [2].

replying_to: Replying to Minimizing Memorization in Meta-learning: A Causal Perspective
display_title: Official Review of Paper2418 by Reviewer 5gbq

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies the memorization overfitting problem in meta-learning from a causal perspective. It provides explanations to current solutions and proposes to update the meta parameters by maximizing the interventional distribution $p(\theta | do(\theta'), S, Q)$. It provides an identification strategy for the interventional distribution by the front door criterion.
content.main_review:
Strength:

- The view of this paper is new. It is interesting to study meta-learning and memorization overfitting from a causal perspective, which is novel. 

- The proposed solution is simple and easy to implement.

- The empirical studies cover four representative examples.

Weakness:

- The connections with existing literature are not explained clearly enough. The memorization overfitting is known as a problem when a single model can solve all the training tasks without using the task support data. This paper describes the memorization as a problem that the ideal target  $\max p(\theta | \theta', S, Q)$ differs from the practical target $\max p(\theta | \theta', S, Q)$. What is the translation between the two descriptions of the same problem?

- The causal graph Figure 1(b) is not very correct with some missing pieces. The current graph implies the query set Q and the support set S are independent, and $\theta'$ and $\theta$ are independent given $Y$, which are not correct.

- In a usual causal graph, the variables are probabilistic. But in the graph of MAML, many relationships are deterministic. Can the author provide a discussion on the probabilistic and deterministic causal graph and also the references for the frontdoor criterion to be applied in the deterministic case?

- Eq (1) and (2) imply that $p(\theta | do(\theta'), Q) = p(\theta | do(\theta'), S, Q)$. By the do-calculus, does it mean $\theta$ independent of S given $\theta'$, Q in the graph $G_{\bar{\theta'}}$? But Figure 1(b) does not imply this conditional independence.

- Some simulation results are not aligned with the previous works. In sec. 5.1 and sec 5.4., the performance of standard MAML is very good. This contradicts with the results in (Farid & Majumdar, 2021) (Rajendran. et al. 2020) (Yin. et al. 2019) that the performance of standard MAML will deteriorate significantly when the tasks are not mutually-exclusive.  

- The sinusoid regression in sec. 5.1 seems not a non-mutually-exclusive version that will induce memorization overfitting.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper provides a novel perspective on the meta-learning and task-level overfitting. However, the reviewer think the motivations need further explanation, the causal graph and identification strategy need scrutiny, and the experimental settings need to be double checked. I would like to hear author's feedback.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5gbq (2/3)
content.comment:
#### Q3: probabilistic vs. deterministic causal graph
> - The first paragraph of Chapter 4 [1] defines that probabilistic causation is used to describe deterministic systems with imperfect knowledge, i.e. unobserved variables. Similarly, Section 2.2 in [2] models a causal graph as a **deterministic function** with arbitrarily distributed random disturbances. Therefore, the probabilistic causal graph is regarded as a deterministic causal graph with only unobserved variables or random disturbances. 
> - In [2], two intervention methods to control confounding bias, i.e., "the backdoor criterion" and "the frontdoor criterion" were proposed. Note that different from the backdoor criterion, the front door criterion is specifically proposed for unobserved confounders (U in Fig. 3 of [2]) so that the variables of confounders do not even appear in the front door criterion (Eq.(9) in [2]). Therefore, the frontdoor criterion is naturally applicable to observed confounders. 
> - In light of 1) our deterministic causal graph characterizing exact deterministic relationship like [2] and 2) the frontdoor criterion proposed in [2] generalizes to observed confounders as in our causal graph, we conclude the validity of deconfounding by the frontdoor criterion in our causal graph. We have included this discussion in Appendix A.2.
>
> [1] (Hitchcock et al. 2020) Hitchcock, Christopher, [Causal Models](https://plato.stanford.edu/archives/sum2020/entries/causal-models/#ProbCausMode), In The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (Summer 2020 Edition).
>
> [2] (Judea. 1995) Pearl Judea. Causal diagrams for empirical research. In Biometrika 1995.

#### Q4: Inconsistency between Eq (1)(2) implying $p(\theta|do(\theta'),Q)=p(\theta|do(\theta'),S,Q)$ and Figure 1(b)
> - We would first of all sincerely apologize for the typo in Eq.(2) and Eq.(4) -- $do(\theta')$ should be corrected to $do(\Phi)$, and Eq.(2) and Eq.(4) exactly correspond to the second part of the first equation in Eq.(1). The correct Eq.(2) and Eq.(4) should be
>   $$
>   p(\theta|do(\Phi), Q)=\int p(\theta|\Phi,\theta_i',Q)p(\theta_i')d\theta_i'\approx\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^M p(\theta|\Phi,\theta_i',Q)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^M p(\theta|\Phi,\theta',Q, z_i),
>   $$
>   and
>   $$
>   p(\theta|do(\Phi), Q) = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{M}p(\theta|\Phi,\theta_m', Q) = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{M}p(\theta|\Phi,\theta', Q, W_m).
>   $$
>   We have corrected both in the revised version.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5gbq (1/3)
content.comment:
We sincerely appreciate your constructive comments to improve our paper. You may find our corresponding explanations below for your concerns. We would really appreciate it if you could let us know if you have any further concerns. 

#### Q1: For the memorization overfitting problem, what is the translation between "a single model can solve all the training tasks without using the task support data" and "the ideal target $\max p(\theta|\theta',S,Q)$ differs from the practical target $\max p(\theta|\theta',S,Q)$"?

> Our causal perspective of the memorization problem where the practical $p(\theta|\theta',S,Q)\rightarrow p(\theta|\theta',Q)$ differs from the ideal $p(\theta|\theta',S,Q)$ properly aligns with the original definition of memorization in [1], in that the learned model ignores the training data (i.e., the support set).
>
> - Definition of the memorization overfitting problem in [1]: complete memorization in meta-learning is when the learned model **ignores** the task training data such that $q(\hat{y}^*|x^*,\theta,\mathcal{D})=q(\hat{y}^*|x^*,\theta)$.
> - Causal perspective of memorization overfitting in our work:
>   - Idea meta-learning: as we have detailed in the last paragraph of Page 3, an ideal meta-learning algorithm will fully adapt the previous meta-knowledge $\theta'$ to a task-specific model $\Phi$ via its support set $S$ in the inner loop, and update the meta-knowledge $\theta$ in the outer loop by evaluating the performance of $\Phi$ on its query set $Q$, i.e., $\theta'\rightarrow \Phi(\leftarrow S)\rightarrow \hat{Y}_{Q}\rightarrow \theta\leftarrow Y$ and $\max p(\theta|\theta',S,Q)$. Note that $Y$ is the groundtruth label of the query set $Q$.
>   - Memorization under non-mutually exclusive settings: as we have detailed in the first paragraph of Page 4, $Y$ in this case also causes $\theta'$. In other words, $Y$ turns into a confounder and opens the backdoor path between $\theta'$ and $\theta$, i.e., $\theta' \leftarrow Y \rightarrow \theta$ (see Figure 1(b) and Figure 2(a)), thereby incurring a **spurious correlation** from $\theta'$ and $\theta$. Such a spurious correlation pushes $\theta$ to directly fit labels $Y$ in query sets $Q$, without going through the real causal path $\theta'\rightarrow \Phi(\leftarrow S)\rightarrow \hat{Y}_{Q}\rightarrow \theta$, i.e., $p(\theta|\theta',S,Q)\rightarrow p(\theta|\theta',Q)$.
>
> [1] (Yin et al. 2020) Mingzhang Yin, George Tucker, Mingyuan Zhou, Sergey Levine, and Chelsea Finn. Meta-learning without memorization. In ICLR 2020.

#### Q2: Causal graph in Figure 1(b)

> Our proposed causal graph in Figure 1(b) implies 
>
> - the independence between the support set $S$ and the query set $Q$, which is consistent with the meta-learning literature [1] and holds in practice where ***i.i.d.* examples** are drawn from a task to constitute its support set $S$ and query set $Q$, respectively.
> - the **non-independence of $\theta'$, $\theta$ given $Y$** actually. There exists the other causal link $\theta'\rightarrow \Phi\rightarrow \hat{Y}_{Q}\rightarrow \theta$ besides the link $\theta' \leftarrow Y \rightarrow \theta$ between $\theta'$ and $\theta$. According to Figure 2(a) which simplifies Figure 1(b) but preserves the causal relationship between $\theta'$, $\theta$ and $Y$, we have $p(\theta,\theta'|Y)=p(\theta|\theta',Y)p(\theta'|Y)\neq p(\theta|Y)p(\theta'|Y)$ that implies that $\theta'$ and $\theta$ are not independent given $Y$. 
>
> [1] (Finn et al. 2017) Chelsea Finn, Pieter Abbeel, and Sergey Levine. Model-agnostic meta-learning for fast adaptation of deep networks. In ICML 2017.
